title: The Venus Knowledge Base
note: Every entry carries a TEST — the thing you could do that would show it false. An entry without one is an opinion with a heading on it. The generator checks that every cited page exists and reports every entry the yard asserts but never demonstrates.

classes.concept: a claim about how things work
classes.mechanism: a technique, and what it costs
classes.figure: a person or a posture, and what it does

settled.settled: demonstrated on a board you can open, and the demonstration is checkable
settled.working: used throughout, argued for, not independently verified
settled.contested: the yard has said two things about it and has not reconciled them

entries.short: No participant reads any other. Removing one changes nothing for the rest.
body: Not "spread out", not "many copies", not "no company owns it". Those are consequences people notice and then mistake for the thing. The property is about READS: a system is decentralised exactly to the extent that no component's behaviour is a function of another component's state.

The automat is the cleanest instance in this yard because it was built to have nothing else in it. Each tribe keeps its own beat, off its own prime, and advances on beats that divide its own period. No tribe queries another. There is no coordinator, no scheduler with a policy, no leader election, no consensus round — the pattern you see on the board is not produced by anything, it is what falls out of several bands not talking.

Which is why removing one is a non-event. Delete a tribe and the remaining ones do not slow down, re-balance, or notice. That is not resilience bolted on afterwards; there is no failure mode to be resilient to, because there was never a dependency to break.
entries.test: Delete one component. If any other component's behaviour changes — timing, output, ordering, anything — it was not decentralised, and the coupling you just found is the real architecture.

evidence.what: 140-odd tribes across 45 boards; no tribe reads another, and the orbit is the lcm rather than a schedule
twelve orders; take one out and the board shows exactly which capabilities stop and which genuinely do not
the network that routes around a cut rather than reporting it

entries.short: No unit is worth more than another, and there is no way to write the function that would prefer one.
body: The test is constructive and it is the whole of the idea: try to write the preference. If you can write a function that ranks two units, they are not fungible, and the ranking is where the rent will be collected. If you cannot write it — not "choose not to", cannot — they are.

This is why the automat has no scoring function. Not as restraint, as a structural fact: there is no goal state to compare an arrangement against, so there is nothing for a ranking to be a ranking of. Every arrangement is reachable from every other and none is worth more, which means there is no arrangement anybody can be induced to reach and none anybody can be charged to leave.

The correction that produced this entry is worth keeping. Early in this repository's life the advice was to add a loss condition and a scarcity to make a game feel like a game. That advice was wrong in a specific way: fungibility exists to remove exactly those two things, and putting them back is not balancing a system, it is un-building it.
entries.test: Write the preference function over two units. If it compiles, they are not fungible. If it does not, ask what the syndicate would have to add before it could — that addition is the attack.

evidence.what: the argument in full: fungibility removes the individual loss condition and the scarcity rent
one substance, two nouns; the matter counter reads 1 on both sides and the capability counter does not
no scoring function, no goal state, no termination test anywhere in the file

entries.term: What it takes to start something
entries.short: Not the most important thing. The smallest closed loop in which every part is fed by another part.
body: The instinct is to start with the root — the biggest, the most depended-upon, the one everything else needs. This yard tested that instinct and it fails, visibly, on a board you can open. Turn on Zeus alone in the twelve-sector economy: nought working, one broken. Add Hera: still nought, still broken. Turn on all four roots — the four sectors with the most downstream dependents — and you get two capabilities and nobody eating.

A root is not a start, because a root is defined by what depends on IT and a start is defined by what feeds IT. Those are different arrows. Something with no inputs produces nothing on its own; it only becomes productive once the things that consume its output exist and return something to it.

So the thing you need is a CYCLE: the smallest set whose members feed each other with no external input required. Not the most important sector — the shortest closed loop. In practice that loop is nearly always unglamorous and involves food, water, and somebody keeping time, because those are the three that everything else quietly assumes. The dependency graph will tell you which loop is shortest; it will not tell you which node is most important, and it does not need to.

The same shape appears in the fourteen terraforming profiles. The envelope has ten downstream dependents — the most of anything on the board — and its own status is only "derived". The most-depended-on thing in the system is a thing nobody has independently established. That is normal, and it is exactly why you do not start there.
entries.test: Invert the dependency graph and look for cycles, not for maxima. If your proposed start has no path back to itself, it is a root and not a start, and it will sit idle producing nothing until you build the return arrow.

evidence.what: Zeus alone: 0 working, 1 broken. All four roots: 2 capabilities, nobody eating
the same twelve, 1,500 years earlier — Nisaba holds grain AND writing, which collapses two nodes into one and shortens the loop
14 requirements, 6 settled; the envelope has 10 downstream and is only derived

entries.short: A scarcity wearing a rule's clothes. And a scarcity is where the rent is collected.
body: A loss condition says: there exists a state from which you cannot continue. That statement creates a last unit — the last life, the last turn, the last chance — and a last unit is by construction scarce. Scarcity is not a feeling about a resource; it is the existence of a final one.

Once a final unit exists, somebody can sell it, and everything downstream follows without anyone intending it: a market in continuation, a price for not-ending, and an incentive to arrange more near-endings. Nobody has to be corrupt for this. The instrument does it.

The corollary is the useful half. Anything genuinely endless cannot be sold by the unit. A quiet storm set has no last record; a superrotation has no last lap; the automat has no last beat. None of them were designed to resist a rent — they simply came out that way, and the resistance is a side-effect of having no final unit to price.
entries.test: Find the last unit. If you can name it — last life, last turn, last block, last lap — ask who would sell it and at what price. If you cannot name one, there is nothing there to rent.

evidence.what: the three notes compiled: a loss condition is a scare factor, compared to something that is and is not at the same time
a format with no arc and a superrotation with no last lap; neither can be sold by the unit
no termination test and no counter that only goes one way

entries.short: De-fungibilisation done entirely in the noun. Nothing is destroyed and four capabilities become four line items.
body: A syndicate does not need to destroy a commons. Destroying things is expensive, visible, and eventually illegal. It needs the commons RENAMED, and then removing it is somebody's contract — renewable, with a schedule of fees.

The forest floor is the demonstration because the substance is identical under both names. Called the floor it is eaten by the beetle, threaded by the fungus, carried as seed, and becomes the tree: four capabilities of the matter itself. Called waste it is hauled, fined, buried, and billed: four services performed on it by somebody with an invoice. The matter counter reads 1 on both sides of the board. The capability counter does not.

And the capabilities are not gone under the second name. They are physically still there — the beetle would still eat it — they are merely unreachable, because it has been hauled somewhere the beetle is not. That is the difference between destruction and enclosure, and enclosure is the cheaper of the two by a wide margin.
entries.test: Hold the substance fixed and change only the noun. If the list of things it can do changes, the change was never about the substance, and somebody is being paid for the difference.

evidence.what: one radio, two nouns, identical matter; matter reads 1 both ways and capability does not
the floor as the tank of seed dispersal — the beetle, the web, the pupation
the structure that profits from the difference

entries.short: Not a bribe. A bribe buys a sentence and can be checked; a retainer buys a full mouth and cannot.
body: The seated figure has his mouth open and a stone in it. He is not corrupt, and insisting on that is the entire value of the image: nobody bought a lie from him, because a lie is a checkable thing and a checkable thing is a liability. He was paid to be FULL.

The instrument has three properties a bribe does not. It contains no false statement anywhere, so it survives an audit. It does not lapse when the mouth closes, so it renews rather than ending. And from outside, an open mouth reads as speech to everyone walking past — which is the exact configuration in which no speech is possible.
Sixteen of the thirty-two arrangements produce a word, which is half of them. Speech is not rare. What is rare is a mouth that is open and empty at the moment somebody is offering to fill it.
entries.test: Look for the false statement. If there is not one, stop looking for corruption and start looking at what the payment is FOR — the answer is usually a capacity rather than an act.

evidence.what: five apertures, 32 arrangements, seven readings; the full mouth is one of them and it is the one you were shown first
the clergy — paid to assist, and the reasons that bind carry nobody's name
the ninth wallet, and what being bound in actually buys

entries.short: The part of an institution's output that is disposable is the part with a name on it. The part that binds has no name on it.
body: A disposal needs a judge. An opinion needs somebody to write it, and nobody on a bench with a real list has the hours. So three clerks draft all twelve opinions, the judges read and correct and sign them, and not one of the twelve carries a drafter's name.

Release the clergy and watch which numbers move. Disposed does not. Fee does not. Every case still ends, on time, at the same price. Drafted and Signed go to nothing. The disposal never needed them; the reasons did.

Which means the sentence that will be quoted across nine thousand square miles of forest for the next forty years was written by somebody on a retainer whom the record does not mention, and the meter that pays for all of it cannot tell a judgment from a plurality. Nobody did anything wrong. That is the problem, and it is the second time that board has had to say so.
entries.test: Remove the assistants and re-run. Whatever still happens on time was never the thing they were doing; whatever stops is what they were actually producing, and you can now check whether their names are on it.

evidence.what: 40 disposals, 12 opinions, 0 bearing a drafter — and `named` is a counter you can watch fail to move
the record, verbatim, which is the only reason any of this can be checked at all

entries.short: Sixteen cards are selected by the circuit. His has no condition on it at all, and that is the finding rather than a shortcut.
body: Every judge on the bench above him reads `.ct:has(#g-po:checked) .jN .vote` — sixteen cards that decide differently depending on what is in front of them, which is what the whole board exists to demonstrate. The Master of the Ordinary List has no `:has()` anywhere. One rule, no condition.

He is not indifferent and he is not lazy. He is fast, he is almost always right, and he is the only reason the other sixteen ever reach a hard case — a court that heard every pot would hear nothing else. But he has taken this question forty times a day for eleven years, and the file stopped being the input somewhere around the four thousandth time.

He is paid per disposal, which is the only line a list can count, so the fee reads identically on the circuits that produce a holding and the ones that produce a plurality with nothing in it. Nothing here is corrupt. It is an accurate meter measuring the wrong quantity, which is worse, because there is nobody to accuse.
And he is not in the division. His forty thousand dispositions appear in none of the court's figures, because the figures were built to count the sixteen.
entries.test: Change the input and watch the output. If a decision-maker's output is invariant across every input you can supply, the input is not what is producing the decision, and you should go looking for what is.

evidence.what: seniority 17 — toggle the twelve circuits and sixteen cards change while his does not

entries.short: A medium moving faster than the thing it rests on, carrying whatever is in it, with no discontinuity in it.
body: A quiet storm set and a Venusian superrotation are the same object described twice. In both the passenger supplies no energy: the set carries the room, the band carries the balloon. Being carried is not a failure to travel — it is the mechanism.

Both are ruined by the same event, which is an ANNOUNCEMENT. The DJ saying the time, or a thruster firing. Either is a discontinuity you can perceive, and the instant there is one you are aware of the mechanism instead of the thing: listening to a radio station, or flying an aircraft. Not carried.
So the craft in both cases is made entirely of what does not happen, which is why it is invisible when it is done well and obvious the moment it is not.
entries.test: Look for the seam. If you can point at a moment where the medium handed off, it is a sequence of events; if you cannot, it is a medium. The listener who can hear the crossfade is no longer inside the format.

evidence.what: seven segments on a 48-column grid, all in row one, overlapping by 14 measured pixels per join
the relay — Venus is not a haul, it is a relay, and a relay has no last leg

entries.short: The solid planet turns once in 243.02 days. The cloud deck laps it in about four and a half.
body: Venus rotates once every 243.02 days, retrograde, with a solar day of 116.75 days. The atmosphere does not go with it: the cloud deck at roughly 65 km is carried at about 100 m/s and circles the entire planet in four to five Earth days. After sixty years of measurement there is no agreed account of what sustains it.

The arithmetic, so it can be checked rather than believed: 6051.8 + 65 = 6116.8 km radius, circumference 38,433 km, at 360 km/h that is 106.8 hours or 4.45 days. Divide 243.02 by 4.45 and you get about 55 laps per solid rotation, or 54 relative to the ground since the body turns the same way.

The figure people quote is sixty. The wind is not one number — it runs roughly 90 to 110 m/s across the deck and varies with latitude and altitude — so the honest statement is four to five days, call it sixty-ish laps, and the honest way to say that is to show the division and let the reader see how loose it is.
entries.test: Do the division yourself with a different wind speed from the published range and see how far the answer moves. If a page gives you one confident figure and no division, it is claiming a precision the measurement does not have.

evidence.what: the arithmetic printed in full, and the gap between the quoted 60 and the computed 55 left visible on purpose
9,000 sq mi as 0.00506% of the surface
116.75 d solar day against a ~4 d super-rotation

entries.short: Carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur are all abundant on Venus. Hydrogen is not, and everything wet depends on it.
body: Venus has carbon and oxygen in enormous quantity, locked in CO₂, and sulphur in the clouds. What it does not have is hydrogen — it is 2.06% by mass of sulphuric acid, and processing a cubic metre of cloud yields almost nothing. Roughly 136,000 m³ of cloud per kilogram of water.

That single fact reorganises the whole settlement problem. Water is not a supply question, it is the supply question, and every other requirement in the fourteen profiles is downstream of whether hydrogen arrives or is extracted. It is also the one genuine scarcity in a system otherwise built to have none, which makes it the place to watch: a real scarcity is where a rent can attach, and this one is real.

The altitude follows from it too. 1.00 bar and 0–50 °C are about five kilometres apart in altitude, and dissolved oxygen moves the settlement from 50 km to 55 km. Tether strength was never the descent problem — 55 km sits inside four fibres' breaking lengths. Heat is, and heat is gradable.
entries.test: Trace any requirement in the profiles back along its inputs. If it terminates at water and the water terminates at hydrogen, it is in the constrained set. If a proposal claims to avoid this, ask where its hydrogen comes from and in what mass.

evidence.what: 2.06% H in H₂SO₄; ~136,000 m³ of cloud per kg of water
the siphon, the cleaning, the healthy waterway
the 9,000 sq mi envelope and what it needs delivered

entries.short: Origin, then layer, then specificity, then source order. Being written last is worth nothing against a heavier selector.
body: This cost the repository a real bug and it is kept written down because a rule that loses looks exactly like a rule nobody wrote. A blanket stop rule at the foot of the ecosystem stylesheet — `.eco:not(:has(#fly:checked)) .cap`, specificity (1,3,0) — was intended to override every capability rule, and every capability rule was a compound `:has()` at (2,4,0). It lost to all of them, silently, and nothing on the screen said so.

The fix was not `!important`. Reaching for importance to win a fight you lost on specificity buries the disagreement rather than settling it, and the next reader inherits a stylesheet whose real precedence is invisible. The fix was noticing the CLAIM WAS FALSE: two of those capabilities genuinely do survive losing the clock, so the blanket rule should never have existed. The arithmetic is still nailed to the foot of that stylesheet as a warning.

The general form is worth more than the CSS. When an override does nothing, the two possibilities are that it lost, or that it was never true. Checking which one costs ten seconds and changes what you do next completely.
entries.test: Compute both specificities. If yours is lower, you lost on specificity and moving the rule will not help. If yours is higher and it still does nothing, your selector never matched — the tree is not what you think it is.

evidence.what: (1,3,0) against (2,4,0), recorded at the foot of the stylesheet rather than quietly fixed
chapters three and four, with the drill that computes both triples
devmode's PROBE, which computes the triple live including :has/:is/:where

entries.short: CSS has no multiplication over state, so you write the products. That is not only a defeat.
body: When an outcome depends on two or three inputs together, there is no expression available — there is a row per combination, and somebody typed every one. Three inputs by four options is twelve rules. Reading × circuit × hour is twenty-four.

The argument for it: every cell is visible, every cell was a decision, and a reviewer can point at row nine and say THAT ONE IS WRONG without reading any logic. An expression hides its cases; a table cannot. When the table gets long enough to hurt, that is information — it means the model has more state than the thing it models deserves, and the answer is usually to cut an input rather than generate the rows.

Know the ceiling before starting. The cost is the product, not the sum: two axes of three is nine and pleasant, three of four is sixty-four and needs a build step, four of five is six hundred and twenty-five and you should have reduced the model. Past about twenty rows this repository generates them from JSON — the page stays scriptless; the authoring does not have to be.
And check first whether you wanted a count rather than a combination. Half the tables people write by hand were a counter.
entries.test: Ask whether the outcome depends on WHICH or on HOW MANY. If how many, it is one counter and no table. If which, count the product before you start typing.

evidence.what: 24 enumerated circuits — reading × circuit × hour × text
17 judges × 12 circuits, and the one card with no condition on it
chapter seven, with the ceiling stated in rows

entries.short: Declare it, increment it with nothing, print it. The only way a stylesheet can state a negative.
body: A sentence saying "no opinion carries a drafter's name" is a claim the reader has to take. A counter named `named`, declared on the body, incremented by no rule anywhere in the file, and printed in the tally, is the same claim in a form the reader can watch fail to move while they change every control on the page.

It is used three times in this yard and it is the same instrument each time: `named` on the bench, `gaps` on the quiet storm set, `burn` on the aerostat riding the air. In each case the interesting number is the one that stays at zero under every setting, and the only way to make a zero legible is to give it somewhere to have gone up.

The cost is that a reader must trust the file — a counter incremented nowhere is indistinguishable from a counter someone forgot to wire. Which is why the pages that use it say so in the stylesheet, in the comment next to the declaration, where the person checking is already looking.
entries.test: Search the stylesheet for the counter's name. If `counter-increment` mentions it anywhere, the zero is a result; if it does not, the zero is an assertion — and the page should say which.

evidence.what: `named` — 40 disposed, 12 drafted, 0 bearing a drafter, under every setting
`gaps` in a set built out of overlaps
the matter counter reading 1 under both nouns while the capability counter moves

entries.term: The half of the URL CSS cannot read
entries.short: CSS reads the fragment through :target. It cannot read the query. Nothing can. So that is where the script layer lives.
body: A document has exactly one `:target` at a time, and the fragment is the only durable state a scriptless page has — it survives reload, it is in the bookmark, it goes in a message, Back is undo. The query string is the other half of the same address and it is invisible to the style layer completely.

That asymmetry is not a limitation to work around, it is a channel. `automat.js` and `devmode.js` are wired into every page in this yard and are inert unless the address carries `?run` or `?dev`. Open a board plainly and nothing runs and the stylesheet decides everything, exactly as before. Open it with a query and a script is pressing the controls — and the two layers cannot collide, because they read different halves of the same URL.
The claim was never that there is no script file. It was that the logic is the cascade, and that is intact and now checkable from inside the page.
entries.test: Open any board without a query string and count the script tags that do anything. Then open it with ?dev and use CENSUS, which counts them for you and says which are inert.

evidence.what: six states, no inputs at all, every control a link — and the query stated as write-only
the channel, and 45 boards driven through it
chapter eight, and the honest answer to wanting two independent durable axes

entries.short: lcm over the tribes of (period × steps). The beats before a board is in an arrangement it has held before.
body: It is the honest measure of an endless thing, and it is computed in two places independently — in the HUD at runtime and in the generator that builds the wall — rather than asserted in either.

It matters because "endless" is cheap to claim. A run whose components all move on period 1 only ever visits the diagonal of its state space and returns to the start almost immediately; it looks endless and is a short loop. Coprime periods make the combined orbit the lcm, which for a board with a sixteen-checkbox bank leaves the safe integers early enough that the arithmetic has to be done in BigInt.
So the number is a claim you can check about a property you would otherwise have to take on faith, which is the same move as the zero counter and the printed division.
entries.test: Set every period to 1 and compute the orbit again. If a system's endlessness survives that, it was structural; if the orbit collapses to the number of steps in one component, the endlessness was the cadences and not the design.

evidence.what: an orbit on every tile, computed from the board's own controls
a set with no last record and a superrotation with no last lap
